power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Anatomy-Aware 3D GAN with Local Mask Renement for Brain MRI Inpainting

text.text: Brain tumor MRI inpainting aims to synthesize plausible healthy-appearing tissue in regions removed from pathological scans.
We present an anatomy-aware three-dimensional generative adversarial network for Task 4 of the BraTS 2026 challenge.

The method combines mask-aware gated convolutions, mirrored contralateral context, attention-modulated skip fusion, boundary-aware renement, and a local masked-region rener, each adapted from established components in the image synthesis and inpainting literature.
The model is trained with a two-stage objective that rst emphasizes voxel-wise and structural reconstruction and then applies low-weight adversarial ne-tuning.
On a deterministic local held-out split, the proposed method substantially improves over a simple 3D AutoEncoder baseline but does not surpass the challenge's Pix2Pix3D baseline.
On the ocial BraTS 2026 Task 4 evaluation server, the submitted model obtained a mean SSIM of 0.658 and a mean PSNR of 14.81 dB over 219 evaluated cases, lower than the local held-out gures.

We report these results transparently, analyze likely contributing factors, and identify the controlled ablations (removal of the mirrored-context channel and of the two-stage schedule) required to isolate the contribution of each architectural component.
Keywords: BraTS • MRI inpainting • local synthesis • generative adversarial networks • 3D convolutional neural networks • brain tumor imaging

The Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) challenge has become a central benchmark for neuro-oncology image analysis, initially focusing on glioma segmentation and later expanding toward multiple tumor entities, clinical settings, and image synthesis tasks [13].
text.formatted: The Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) challenge has become a central benchmark for neuro-oncology image analysis, initially focusing on glioma segmentation and later expanding toward multiple tumor entities, clinical settings, and image synthesis tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Task 4 of the BraTS 2026 challenge addresses local synthesis or inpainting of brain tumor MRI scans, where the goal is to reconstruct healthy-appearing tissue in regions removed from a pathological T1-normalized image.

This task is motivated by the need to make tumor-bearing scans more compatible with algorithms developed for healthy or non-lesional brain images, including parcellation, tissue segmentation, image registration, and downstream morphometric analysis [4].
text.formatted: This task is motivated by the need to make tumor-bearing scans more compatible with algorithms developed for healthy or non-lesional brain images, including parcellation, tissue segmentation, image registration, and downstream morphometric analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Medical image inpainting diers from natural image completion in several important ways.
First, the result must be anatomically plausible in three dimensions rather than only visually coherent in a two-dimensional projection.
Second, output intensities must remain consistent with the original scan so that the synthesized region does not introduce articial discontinuities.
Third, the prediction must not alter the known non-masked tissue, because unnecessary changes outside the target region may invalidate the output for downstream analysis.
Finally, the evaluation region is explicitly dened by a binary mask, making the challenge objective highly localized.
The challenge baseline includes a 3D AutoEncoder and a 3D Pix2Pix-style model.
Pix2Pix introduced conditional adversarial learning for paired imageto-image translation and remains a strong reference for synthesis problems [5].
text.formatted: Pix2Pix introduced conditional adversarial learning for paired imageto-image translation and remains a strong reference for synthesis problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: However, direct adversarial optimization can sometimes reduce voxel-wise similarity metrics when the discriminator encourages visually plausible but numerically shifted outputs.

For the inpainting challenge, where metrics include structural similarity index measure (SSIM), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), mean squared error (MSE), and root mean squared error (RMSE), reconstruction accuracy remains central [6].
text.formatted: For the inpainting challenge, where metrics include structural similarity index measure (SSIM), peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), mean squared error (MSE), and root mean squared error (RMSE), reconstruction accuracy remains central <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: We investigate AnatomyAwareGAN3D, a three-dimensional inpainting model that combines the binary mask, approximate left-right brain symmetry, boundary supervision, and local masked-region renement into a single architecture.

Rather than proposing new individual components, our contribution lies in adapting and combining several established techniques from the general imagesynthesis literature gated convolutions [7], attention-gated skip connections [8], residual learning [9], and spectral normalization [10] for the specic constraints of masked 3D MRI inpainting, where only a small, explicitly dened sub-volume is evaluated.
text.formatted: Rather than proposing new individual components, our contribution lies in adapting and combining several established techniques from the general imagesynthesis literature gated convolutions <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>, attention-gated skip connections <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>, residual learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>, and spectral normalization <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> for the specic constraints of masked 3D MRI inpainting, where only a small, explicitly dened sub-volume is evaluated.

text.text: We evaluate this combination on a local held-out split against the challenge's own AutoEncoder and Pix2Pix3D baselines and report the result candidly, including that the method does not yet close the gap to Pix2Pix3D.
We also report the score returned by the ocial challenge evaluation server for our submitted container.
Our contributions are as follows:

We adapt gated convolutions, mirrored contralateral context, attention-modulated skip fusion, boundary renement, and local masked-region renement each grounded in prior work into a single 3D generator for mask-constrained MRI inpainting.

We describe a two-stage training strategy that combines masked L1, SSIM, multi-scale masked L1, boundary-ring loss, and low-weight adversarial netuning, and we report checkpoint selection by two dierent validation criteria.
We provide a compact Docker inference pipeline that preserves the original non-masked tissue and writes challenge-compliant NIfTI outputs.

We evaluate the model on a deterministic local held-out split, compare against AutoEncoder and Pix2Pix3D baselines, report the ocial server-side score of the submitted model, and explicitly identify the ablations needed to attribute performance to individual architectural choices, which remain as future work.
2 Related Work
BraTS has played a major role in standardizing brain tumor MRI analysis by providing curated multimodal datasets, benchmark tasks, and common evaluation protocols [1, 2].
text.formatted: BraTS has played a major role in standardizing brain tumor MRI analysis by providing curated multimodal datasets, benchmark tasks, and common evaluation protocols <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: The 2026 challenge extends this tradition through multiple tasks that address segmentation, generalizability, pathology-related prediction, and local synthesis [3].
text.formatted: The 2026 challenge extends this tradition through multiple tasks that address segmentation, generalizability, pathology-related prediction, and local synthesis <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: The inpainting task is especially relevant because tumorbearing anatomy often breaks assumptions made by tools developed for healthy subjects.
The BraTS local synthesis task was introduced to encourage methods that can replace tumor-aected or removed tissue with plausible healthy tissue [4].
text.formatted: The BraTS local synthesis task was introduced to encourage methods that can replace tumor-aected or removed tissue with plausible healthy tissue <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Unlike segmentation, where the output is a label map, inpainting requires voxel-level synthesis of a continuous intensity image.
This makes the task sensitive to intensity normalization, boundary blending, and contextual consistency.
Strong inpainting models must infer missing anatomy while preserving the identity of the scan outside the mask.
Generative adversarial networks (GANs) introduced a framework for training generators using learned discriminators [11].
text.formatted: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) introduced a framework for training generators using learned discriminators <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: Conditional GANs, including Pix2Pix, extended this idea to paired image-to-image translation [5].
text.formatted: Conditional GANs, including Pix2Pix, extended this idea to paired image-to-image translation <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Least-squares GANs improved stability by replacing binary cross-entropy with a regression-style adversarial objective [12].
text.formatted: Least-squares GANs improved stability by replacing binary cross-entropy with a regression-style adversarial objective <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: Our model uses a conditional adversarial loss only during ne-tuning and keeps the adversarial weight small, because the target challenge metrics reward similarity to hidden ground truth rather than unrestricted perceptual realism.
The generator and discriminator components used in this paper are individually well established, and we position each explicitly rather than presenting them as novel.

Gated convolutions were introduced for free-form image inpainting to let the network learn a dynamic, per-location feature gate conditioned on the mask, which also mitigates the color-discrepancy and blurry-boundary artifacts common to plain-convolution inpainting networks [7]; we adopt this mechanism directly for the 3D setting.
text.formatted: Gated convolutions were introduced for free-form image inpainting to let the network learn a dynamic, per-location feature gate conditioned on the mask, which also mitigates the color-discrepancy and blurry-boundary artifacts common to plain-convolution inpainting networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>; we adopt this mechanism directly for the 3D setting.

text.text: Attention-gated skip connections were proposed in Attention U-Net to suppress irrelevant encoder activations before they are fused into the decoder, originally for pancreas segmentation [8]; we reuse the same gating principle, conditioning the attention map additionally on the inpainting mask so that skip features near the voided region are down-weighted unless the decoder attends to them.
text.formatted: Attention-gated skip connections were proposed in Attention U-Net to suppress irrelevant encoder activations before they are fused into the decoder, originally for pancreas segmentation <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>; we reuse the same gating principle, conditioning the attention map additionally on the inpainting mask so that skip features near the voided region are down-weighted unless the decoder attends to them.

text.text: Residual connections follow the formulation of He et al. [9] and are used throughout the bottleneck to stabilize gradient ow in a deep 3D network.
text.formatted: Residual connections follow the formulation of He et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> and are used throughout the bottleneck to stabilize gradient ow in a deep 3D network.

text.text: The discriminator uses spectral normalization [10] to bound its Lipschitz constant and stabilize adversarial ne-tuning.
text.formatted: The discriminator uses spectral normalization <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> to bound its Lipschitz constant and stabilize adversarial ne-tuning.

text.text: U-Net-style encoder-decoder architectures with skip connections [13] and their 3D extension [14] form the backbone on which these components are assembled.
text.formatted: U-Net-style encoder-decoder architectures with skip connections <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> and their 3D extension <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> form the backbone on which these components are assembled.

text.text: The novelty of our approach is therefore the specic combination and mask-conditioning of these established components for localized 3D MRI inpainting, not the individual mechanisms themselves.

Regarding the mirrored-context channel, approximate left-right structural symmetry of the human brain is a documented, though imperfect, anatomical property: healthy brain hemispheres show strong but not exact correspondence, with well-characterized regions of structural and functional asymmetry [15].
text.formatted: Regarding the mirrored-context channel, approximate left-right structural symmetry of the human brain is a documented, though imperfect, anatomical property: healthy brain hemispheres show strong but not exact correspondence, with well-characterized regions of structural and functional asymmetry <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: We use this property only as a weak prior an additional input channel the network may draw on rather than as an assumption enforced on the output, and we discuss its limitations under pathology in Sect. 5; we treat this as an open question rather than a demonstrated result (see Sect.

The results indicate that the combination of components in AnatomyAware-GAN3D substantially outperforms a simple AutoEncoder baseline on our local split.
As noted in Sect.

4.3, however, we cannot currently attribute this improvement to any specic component the mirrored-context channel, attentionmodulated skip fusion, boundary renement, or the two-stage training schedule without the ablations described there, and we present the method as a combination whose net eect we measured, not as a set of individually validated contributions.
The method does not exceed the Pix2Pix3D baseline on the local split.
Because both methods are evaluated on the identical xed split described in Sect.

4.1, this gap cannot be attributed to properties of the split itself, since any such eect would apply equally to both models; the more likely explanations are dierences in eective model capacity, optimization schedule, or the specic inductive biases each architecture encodes, none of which we have isolated experimentally.
The ocial server-side result tempers the local ndings.
On the ocial cases the model scores a mean SSIM of 0.658 and PSNR of 14.81 dB, well below its local held-out values, which shows that the local split overestimated performance on the ocial data.
We have not isolated the cause.

Plausible contributors include dierences between the ocial cases and our local split (for example in mask size, location or scanner characteristics), dierences between our local metric implementation and the server's evaluation code, and overtting of checkpoint selection to the local split; none of these has been tested here.

The ocial SSIM is numerically closer to our local AutoEncoder result than to the local Pix2Pix3D result, but because the two evaluations dier in cases and possibly in metric implementation, this should not be read as a ranking.
Evaluating the baselines on the ocial cases, or re-scoring our model and the baselines with the server's metric code on our local split, would resolve this and is a priority for future work.

The reliance on the mirrored-context channel is motivated by documented, approximate bilateral symmetry of the brain [15], but this symmetry is known to be imperfect and can be locally violated by the tumor and surgical or lesionrelated tissue changes that motivate the inpainting task in the rst place; in cases with substantial mass eect or midline shift, the mirrored channel could plausibly provide misleading rather than helpful context.

text.text: We ag this as an open question rather than a settled design choice, to be resolved by the ablation in Sect.
4.3 together with a qualitative review of failure cases stratied by mask laterality and size.
A further limitation is the xed 128 × 128 × 96 crop size (Sect.
3.2), chosen empirically rather than derived from a reported distribution of mask sizes in the training set; very large or irregular masks may exceed the eld of view available to the network.

Reporting the actual mask-size distribution against the xed crop, and evaluating performance stratied by mask size, would clarify how often this limitation is encountered in practice and is left for future work alongside the ablations above.
The Dockerized inference pipeline (Sect.

3.9) preserves the non-masked region exactly and modies only the mask, which reduces the risk of invalid outputs and satises the challenge's one-le-per-case requirement, but is an implementation detail of challenge compliance rather than a scientic contribution, and we do not present it as one.

6 Conclusion We investigated AnatomyAwareGAN3D, a 3D generator for local synthesis of brain MRI tissue in the BraTS 2026 inpainting task, combining gated convolutions, mirrored contralateral context, attention-modulated skip fusion, boundaryaware renement, multi-scale reconstruction losses, and a local masked-region rener each adapted from established prior work rather than proposed as novel individually.
On a local held-out split, the combination improves substantially over an AutoEncoder baseline but does not surpass the stronger Pix2Pix3D baseline.
On the ocial challenge server the submitted model obtained a mean SSIM of 0.658 and PSNR of 14.81 dB over 219 cases, below its local held-out performance.

We report these outcomes directly rather than overstating it, and we identify the two controlled ablations removing the mirrored-context channel and removing the two-stage training schedule required to attribute the observed gain to specic components, together with mask-size-stratied evaluation and multi-fold variability reporting, as concrete next steps before any claim of component-level contribution can be supported.
